clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant axonal Charcot-Marie-Tooth neuropathy caused by mutations in HSPB1, which encodes the small heat shock protein HSP27, a stress-inducible molecular chaperone abundant in neurons.

Allelic with distal hereditary motor neuropathy type 2B (dHMN2B): the same HSPB1 mutations may produce a purely motor phenotype in some family members and a CMT2 phenotype with sensory involvement in others.
Typical presentation is adult-onset, length-dependent, distal lower-limb weakness and wasting with foot drop, pes cavus and depressed ankle reflexes.
The neuropathy is characteristically motor-predominant, with sensory signs relatively mild or absent, unlike many other CMT2 subtypes.
Nerve conduction studies show a primary axonal pattern with reduced compound muscle action potential amplitudes and preserved or only mildly slowed conduction velocities.
Most pathogenic changes cluster in the conserved alpha-crystallin domain of HSP27, impairing chaperone function.
Mutant HSP27 disrupts assembly and axonal transport of neurofilaments, producing the length-dependent motor axon degeneration.
Diagnosis rests on the pedigree, the axonal electrophysiology and confirmatory HSPB1 sequencing rather than nerve biopsy.
reference.pathophysiology: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2F is an autosomal dominant, primarily axonal peripheral neuropathy caused by heterozygous mutations in HSPB1 (chromosome 7), the gene encoding heat shock protein beta-1 (HSP27). HSP27 is a stress-inducible small heat shock protein that acts as an ATP-independent molecular chaperone, prevents aggregation of misfolded proteins, and regulates cytoskeletal dynamics. In neurons it interacts with neurofilaments and the microtubule network to maintain axonal transport. Most disease-causing variants lie within the highly conserved alpha-crystallin domain and act through a combination of loss of chaperone activity and toxic gain of function: mutant HSP27 promotes hyperphosphorylation and aggregation of neurofilaments, disorganises the axonal cytoskeleton and impairs anterograde and retrograde transport. Because the longest motor axons are most vulnerable to failing transport, the result is a length-dependent, motor-predominant axonopathy that clinically overlaps with distal hereditary motor neuropathy, with which CMT2F is allelic.
additionalDifferentials: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2E (NEFL, neurofilament light chain), which similarly disrupts neurofilament networks
Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2A (MFN2), the commonest axonal CMT
Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2D (GARS) and other aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase neuropathies
Distal hereditary motor neuropathy of other genetic causes (a purely motor mimic)
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis or other motor neuron disease when the phenotype is strongly motor-predominant
additionalInvestigations: Nerve conduction studies and electromyography to confirm a length-dependent axonal, motor-predominant pattern
Targeted HSPB1 sequencing or a hereditary neuropathy gene panel
Detailed three-generation pedigree to establish dominant inheritance and variable expressivity
Clinical sensory examination to document the relative sparing of large-fibre sensation
Serum studies to exclude acquired axonal neuropathy (for example diabetes and other metabolic causes)
Nerve biopsy only in atypical cases, showing chronic axonal loss without primary demyelination
redFlags: Rapidly progressive weakness over weeks to months, which is atypical and should prompt search for an acquired cause
Upper motor neuron signs (spasticity, brisk reflexes, extensor plantar responses) suggesting motor neuron disease rather than CMT2F
Prominent bulbar, respiratory or proximal weakness out of keeping with a length-dependent neuropathy
Early, severe sensory loss or sensory ataxia that points away from this motor-predominant subtype
reference.prognosis: CMT2F is typically slowly progressive with adult onset, and most affected individuals retain independent ambulation with orthotic support and have a normal life expectancy. Disability is dominated by distal motor deficit and foot deformity rather than sensory loss.
pitfalls: The motor-predominant picture and near-normal conduction velocities can lead to misdiagnosis as motor neuron disease or a generic distal myopathy.
Because HSPB1 mutations are allelic with distal hereditary motor neuropathy, absence of sensory signs does not exclude the diagnosis.
Preserved conduction velocities may be wrongly interpreted as excluding a hereditary neuropathy, delaying genetic testing.
Marked intrafamilial variability means clinically silent or mildly affected carriers may be missed on examination alone.
